{{short description|On four non-intersecting circles that lie inside  a bigger circle and tangent to it}}
In [[mathematics]], '''Casey's theorem''', also known as the generalized [[Ptolemy's theorem]], is a theorem in [[Euclidean geometry]] named after the Irish [[mathematician]] [[John Casey (mathematician)|John Casey]]. In [[Japanese mathematics|Wasan]], it is said to have been discovered roughly thirty years before Casey’s publication<ref>{{Cite journal |last=三上 |first=義夫 |date=1919 |title=日本數學上ニ於ケル Casey ノ定理 |url=https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/tmj1911/15/0/15_0_289/_article/-char/ja |journal=Tohoku Mathematical Journal |series=First Series |volume=15 |pages=289–296}}</ref>.

== Formulation of the theorem==

[[File:Casey new1a.svg|thumb|upright=1.25|<math>t_{12} \cdot t_{34}+t_{14}\cdot t_{23}-t_{13}\cdot t_{24}=0 </math>]]

Let <math>\,O</math> be a circle of radius <math>\,R</math>. Let <math>\,O_1, O_2, O_3, O_4</math> be (in that order) four non-intersecting circles that lie inside <math>\,O</math> and tangent to it. Denote by <math>\,t_{ij}</math> the length of the exterior common [[bitangent]] of the circles <math>\,O_i, O_j</math>. Then:<ref name="Cas"/>

:<math>\,t_{12} \cdot t_{34}+t_{14} \cdot t_{23}=t_{13}\cdot t_{24}.</math>

Note that in the degenerate case, where all four circles reduce to points, this is exactly Ptolemy's theorem.

== Proof ==

The following proof is attributable<ref name="Bot"/> to Zacharias.<ref name="Zach"/> Denote the radius of circle <math>\,O_i</math> by <math>\,R_i</math> and its tangency point with the circle <math>\,O</math> by <math>\,K_i</math>. We will use the notation <math>\,O, O_i</math> for the centers of the circles.
Note that from [[Pythagorean theorem]],

:<math>\,t_{ij}^2=\overline{O_iO_j}^2-(R_i-R_j)^2.</math>

We will try to express this length in terms of the points <math>\,K_i,K_j</math>. By the [[law of cosines]] in triangle <math>\,O_iOO_j</math>,

:<math>\overline{O_iO_j}^2=\overline{OO_i}^2+\overline{OO_j}^2-2\overline{OO_i}\cdot \overline{OO_j}\cdot \cos\angle O_iOO_j</math>

Since the circles <math>\,O,O_i</math> tangent to each other:

:<math>\overline{OO_i} = R - R_i,\, \angle O_iOO_j = \angle K_iOK_j</math>

Let <math>\,C</math> be a point on the circle <math>\,O</math>. According to the [[law of sines]] in triangle <math>\,K_iCK_j</math>:

:<math>\overline{K_iK_j} = 2R\cdot \sin\angle K_iCK_j = 2R\cdot \sin\frac{\angle K_iOK_j}{2}</math>

Therefore,

:<math>\cos\angle K_iOK_j = 1-2\sin^2\frac{\angle K_iOK_j}{2}=1-2\cdot \left(\frac{\overline{K_iK_j}}{2R}\right)^2 = 1 - \frac{\overline{K_iK_j}^2}{2R^2}</math>

and substituting these in the formula above:

:<math>\overline{O_iO_j}^2=(R-R_i)^2+(R-R_j)^2-2(R-R_i)(R-R_j)\left(1-\frac{\overline{K_iK_j}^2}{2R^2}\right)</math>

:<math>\overline{O_iO_j}^2=(R-R_i)^2+(R-R_j)^2-2(R-R_i)(R-R_j)+(R-R_i)(R-R_j)\cdot \frac{\overline{K_iK_j}^2}{R^2}</math>

:<math>\overline{O_iO_j}^2=((R-R_i)-(R-R_j))^2+(R-R_i)(R-R_j)\cdot \frac{\overline{K_iK_j}^2}{R^2}</math>

And finally, the length we seek is

:<math>t_{ij}=\sqrt{\overline{O_iO_j}^2-(R_i-R_j)^2}=\frac{\sqrt{R-R_i}\cdot \sqrt{R-R_j}\cdot \overline{K_iK_j}}{R}</math>

We can now evaluate the left hand side, with the help of the original Ptolemy's theorem applied to the inscribed [[quadrilateral]] <math>\,K_1K_2K_3K_4</math>:

:<math>
\begin{align}
& t_{12}t_{34}+t_{14}t_{23} \\[4pt]
= {} & \frac{1}{R^2}\cdot \sqrt{R-R_1}\sqrt{R-R_2}\sqrt{R-R_3}\sqrt{R-R_4} \left(\overline{K_1K_2} \cdot \overline{K_3K_4}+\overline{K_1K_4}\cdot \overline{K_2K_3}\right) \\[4pt]
= {} & \frac{1}{R^2}\cdot \sqrt{R-R_1}\sqrt{R-R_2}\sqrt{R-R_3}\sqrt{R-R_4}\left(\overline{K_1K_3}\cdot \overline{K_2K_4}\right) \\[4pt]
= {} & t_{13}t_{24}
\end{align}
</math>

==Further generalizations ==

It can be seen that the four circles need not lie inside the big circle. In fact, they may be tangent to it from the outside as well. In that case, the following change should be made:<ref name="John"/>
:
If <math>\,O_i, O_j</math> are both tangent from the same side of <math>\,O</math> (both in or both out), <math>\,t_{ij}</math> is the length of the exterior common tangent.
:
If <math>\,O_i, O_j</math> are tangent from different sides of <math>\,O</math> (one in and one out), <math>\,t_{ij}</math> is the length of the interior common tangent.
:
The converse of Casey's theorem is also true.<ref name="John"/> That is, if equality holds, the circles are tangent to a common circle.

==Applications==

Casey's theorem and its converse can be used to prove a variety of statements in [[Euclidean geometry]]. For example, the shortest known proof<ref name="Cas"/>{{rp|411}} of [[Feuerbach's theorem]] uses the converse theorem.
